'''Christopher Michael Reddy''' (born 1969) is a senior scientist in the Department of Marine Chemistry & Geochemistry of the [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]] (WHOI) and faculty member of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]-[[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution|WHOI]] Joint Program in Oceanography/Applied Ocean Science and Engineering.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.whoi.edu/what-we-do/understand/departments-centers-labs/mcg/?_gl=1*1tbdsmi*_gcl_au*Mzc5MTUyNTAxLjE3MzY0MDk1ODU.*_ga*MTQ0NzkyNDk1NS4xNzM2NDA5NTg2*_ga_HLKFZX9JZK*MTczNjQzNTg4NC4yLjAuMTczNjQzNTg4NC4wLjAuMA..| title=Marine Chemistry & Geochemistry | website=whoi.educ}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://mit.whoi.edu/academics/fields/chemical-oceanography/co-faculty/ |title=Faculty : MIT/WHOI Joint Program |website=mit.whoi.edu}}</ref> 

Reddy's research includes the source, fate, and transport of combustion-derived materials, [[PCBs]], and [[DDT]]; the environmental chemistry of [[oil spill]]s, [[biofuel]]s, [[Plastic pollution|plastics]], and [[nanoparticle]]s; and the development of environmentally friendly products. He is considered a leading scientist on [[oil spills]] and conducted an in-depth and long-term investigation into the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill|''Deepwater Horizon'' oil spill]] and its long-term aftereffects.<ref name="Bourzac">{{cite journal |last1=Bourzac |first1=Katherine |title='I remind people all the time that science can wait' |journal=Nature |date=25 September 2023 |doi=10.1038/d41586-023-03022-5 |pmid=37749343 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-03022-5 |access-date=14 January 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

Reddy holds eleven U.S. patents.<ref>{{cite web |title=Christopher M. Reddy |url=https://patents.google.com/?q=(%22C.+M.+Reddy%22)&inventor=%22Christopher+Reddy%22%2c&oq=%22Christopher+Reddy%22%2c+%22C.+M.+Reddy%22 |website=Google Patents |access-date=21 January 2025}}</ref> He has testified before the [[United States Congress|U.S. Congress]] five times, written more than 20 opinion pieces, and given hundreds of interviews for print, radio, and television. Reddy gave a [[TEDx]] talk on the role of science in a crisis.<ref name="star trek">{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kzeBNjHdBzc | title=Communicating Science Through Star Trek | via=YouTube| date=18 November 2011 }}</ref> A newly discovered microbe that can aid in the breakdown of hydrocarbons was named in his honor.

==Early life and education==

Reddy grew up on Rhode Island’s [[Narragansett Bay]] and has always lived within a few miles of the coast. After attending public schools in [[Rhode Island]], Reddy earned a BS in chemistry with a minor in mathematics from [[Rhode Island College]], graduating in 1992.<ref name="WHOI writeup">{{cite web |title=Christopher Reddy, Marine Chemist |url=https://www.whoi.edu/news-insights/content/christopher-reddy-marine-chemist/ |website=whoi.edu |publisher=WHOI |access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref> While there, he was named the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Outstanding Undergraduate Student in 1991.<ref name="CV">{{cite web |title=CURRICULUM VITAE |url=https://www2.whoi.edu/site/chrisreddylab/wp-content/uploads/sites/81/2020/12/REddy-extended-CV-dec-10-2020fin.pdf |website=whoi.edu |publisher=WHOI |access-date=16 January 2025}}</ref> In 1997, he was awarded a PhD in [[chemical oceanography]] from the Graduate School of Oceanography at the [[University of Rhode Island]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Christopher M. Reddy, Senior Scientist |url=https://www2.whoi.edu/site/chrisreddylab/?_gl=1%2Achxg4h%2A_gcl_au%2AMzc5MTUyNTAxLjE3MzY0MDk1ODU.%2A_ga%2AMTQ0NzkyNDk1NS4xNzM2NDA5NTg2%2A_ga_HLKFZX9JZK%2AMTczNjkyOTA2Mi4xMi4xLjE3MzY5MjkwNzYuMC4wLjA. |website=whoi.edu |publisher=WHOI |access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref> While a graduate student, he was named the American Chemical Society's Outstanding Graduate Student in [[Environmental chemistry|Environmental Chemistry]].<ref name="CV" />

==Career highlights==

After receiving his BS in 1992, Reddy worked as a chemist for ULTRA Scientific in North Kingstown, RI, and then as an environmental chemist for CEIMIC Corporation located in Narragansett, RI, from 1993 through 1994. While earning his PhD at [[University of Rhode Island|URI]], he worked as a research graduate assistant in chemical oceanography.

Reddy began his employment with [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]]'s Department of Marine Chemistry and Geochemistry in 1997 after earning his PhD and has remained there since, as a post-doctoral scholar and investigator (1997–2000), assistant scientist (2000–2004), associate scientist (2004–2006), associate scientist with tenure (2006–2010), and senior scientist (2010–present). Also at WHOI, he was manager of the WHOI Small Boats Fleet from 2008–2014 and director of the Coastal [[Ocean Institute]] from 2008–2015. 

During his time with WHOI, Reddy has also been a visiting scholar at [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] at [[University of California, San Diego|UC San Diego]], [[La Jolla, CA]], in 2003 and a visiting associate at the [[California Institute of Technology]]'s Division of Geologic and Planetary Sciences located in [[Pasadena, CA]], in 2005.<ref name="CV" />

==Research areas==

===Oil spills===

Reddy is best known for his and his team’s research into “the processes that regulate the fate of petroleum following release to the environment” and for the invention of the application of [[comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography]] (GCxGC) that enables identification of these processes<ref name="Eglinton" /> which Reddy patented.<ref name="patent" /> 

As it degrades in a marine environment, oil undergoes complex transformations, producing residues composed of extremely complex organic mixtures that accumulate in protective environments<ref name="Eglinton">{{cite journal |last1=Eglinton |first1=Timothy L. |title=Citation for presentation of the 2014 C.C. Patterson Award to Christopher M. Reddy |journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta |date=January 2016 |volume=172 |pages=458–60 |doi=10.1016/j.gca.2015.11.035|bibcode=2016GeCoA.172..458E }}</ref> such as those afforded by fiddler crabs<ref name=“crabs”>{{cite journal |last1=Culbertson |first1=Jennifer B. |last2=Valiela |first2=Ivan |last3=Peacock |first3=Emily E. |last4=Reddy |first4=Christopher M. |last5=Carter |first5=Anna |last6=VanderKruik |first6=Rachel |title=Long-term biological effects of petroleum residues on fiddler crabs in salt marshes |journal=Marine Pollution Bulletin |year=2007 |volume=54 |issue=7 |pages=955–62 |doi=10.1016/j.marpolbul.2007.02.015 |pmid=17448504|bibcode=2007MarPB..54..955C |hdl=1912/1802 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and marsh grass.<ref name=“grass”>{{cite journal |last1=Culbertson |first1=Jennifer B. |last2=Valiela |first2=Ivan |last3=Pickart |first3=Matthew |last4=Peacock |first4=Emily E. |last5=Reddy |first5=Christopher M. |title=Long-term consequences of residual petroleum on salt marsh grass |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |date=9 July 2008 |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=1284–92 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2664.2008.01477.x|bibcode=2008JApEc..45.1284C }}</ref> These residues form the majority of the [[unresolved complex mixture]] (UCM) resulting from the breakdown of crude oils which [[gas chromatography|GC]] had previously been unable to resolve but which Reddy’s novel GCxGC application has made accessible, enabling determination of “the underlying processes controlling petroleum fate” as it degrades in a marine environment.<ref name="Eglinton" /> For this invention, Reddy was awarded the Clair C. Patterson Award in 2014 by the [[Geochemical Society]] for "an innovative breakthrough in environmental geochemistry of fundamental significance within the last decade, particularly in service to society. To be viewed as innovative, the work must show a high degree of creativity and/or be a fundamental departure from usual practice while contributing significantly to understanding in environmental geochemistry."<ref name="Patterson" />

Reddy's investigation into an oil spill that had occurred along West Falmouth Harbor, Massachusetts, in 1969 revealed chemical and biological effects that had persisted even after 30 years<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Reddy |first1=Christopher M. |last2=Eglinton |first2=Timothy I. |last3=Hounshell |first3=Aubrey |last4=White |first4=Helen K. |last5=Xu |first5=Li |last6=Gaines |first6=Richard B. |last7=Frysinger |first7=Glenn S. |title=The West Falmouth Oil Spill after Thirty Years: The Persistence of Petroleum Hydrocarbons in Marsh Sediments |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |date=27 September 2002 |volume=36 |issue=22 |pages=4754–60 |doi=10.1021/es020656n|pmid=12487296 |bibcode=2002EnST...36.4754R }}</ref> in fiddler crabs<ref name=“crabs” /> and [[salt marsh]] grass.<ref name=“grass” /> The results of this study, which lasted from 1999 to 2008, led to significant advances in [[oil spill]] remediation.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hentz |first1=Daniel |title=Fifty years later, the West Falmouth oil spill yields lasting contributions to remediation efforts |url=https://www.whoi.edu/news-insights/content/fifty-years-later-the-west-falmouth-oil-spill/ |website=who.edu |publisher=WHOI |access-date=14 January 2025 |location=Woods Hole, MA |date=20 September 2019}}</ref> Similarly, Reddy and the WHOI chemistry team conducted an extensive study of the [[Bouchard Oil Spill]], which occurred in Massachusetts’ [[Buzzards Bay]] in 2003, using GCxGC.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nelson |first1=Robert K. |last2=Kile |first2=Brian M. |last3=Plata |first3=Desiree L. |last4=Silva |first4=Sean P. |last5=Xu |first5=Li |last6=Reddy |first6=Christopher M. |last7=Gaines |first7=Richard B. |last8=Frysinger |first8=Glenn S. |last9=Reichenbach |first9=Stephen E. |title=Tracking the weathering of an oil spill with comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography |journal=Environmental Forensics |date=March 2006 |volume=7 |issue=1 Reddy and his team were some of the first chemists involved in the 2010 ''[[Deepwater Horizon]]'' disaster in the [[Gulf of Mexico]] and spent the following ~10 years investigating the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill|''Deepwater Horizon'' oil spill]] and its aftermath. Reddy and his team members were unfortunately drawn into the ensuing legal aspects of the spill when the [[U.S. Government]] used the data he and his team had collected to determine how much [[BP]] owed by way of restitution. BP challenged the amount of this restitution and requested Reddy's and his team members' emails and personal correspondence for the time period over which they had studied the spill, a request with which they were reluctantly forced to comply in 2011 following litigation. The ''Deepwater Horizon'' spill also led to one of Reddy's appearances before the [[U.S. Congress]], testifying on 15 June 2010 regarding government agencies' preparedness to respond to crises such as ''Deepwater Horizon''.<ref name="Bourzac" />

Reddy is currently working with UC Santa Barbara researchers to investigate natural oil seepage from the ocean floor off the coast of California.<ref name="WHOI writeup" />

To honor Reddy’s contributions to the study of oil spills, a newly discovered marine microbe capable of degrading branched [[alkane]]s was named ''Candidatus Reddybacter'' in his honor.<ref name="reddybacter" />

===Other research===

In addition to oil spills, Reddy is engaged in research related to degradation of other chemicals and plastics that have been dumped or spilled in the ocean (e.g., the 2021 [[Plastic resin pellet pollution|nurdle]] spill off the coast of Sri Lanka<ref name="nurdles" />), development of biofuels,<ref>{{cite web |title=Chris Reddy Lab: Projects |url=https://www2.whoi.edu/site/chrisreddylab/oil-spill-research/oil-in-our-coastal-back-yard/projects/?_gl=1*11gi24n*_gcl_au*Mzc5MTUyNTAxLjE3MzY0MDk1ODU.*_ga*MTQ0NzkyNDk1NS4xNzM2NDA5NTg2*_ga_HLKFZX9JZK*MTczNjk4NTY0NC4xNi4xLjE3MzY5ODU5NjEuMC4wLjA. |website=whoi.edu |publisher=WHOI |access-date=16 January 2025}}</ref> replacement of hydrocarbons from fossil fuels in personal care products with chemicals derived from marine algae,<ref>{{cite news |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=13 July 2023 |title=Lipsticks, shampoo from algae: Woods Hole company intends to disrupt personal care market |url=https://www.capecodtimes.com/story/business/2023/07/13/upwell-cosmetics-cosmetic-industry-algae-woods-hole-oceanographic-institution-lipstick/70347804007/ |location=Hyannis, MA |work=Cape Cod Times |access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref> and design of safer and more sustainable plastics.<ref name="ACS2024">{{cite press release |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=7 September 2023 |title=Christopher M. Reddy honored with ACS 2024 Grady-Stack award |url=https://www.acs.org/pressroom/newsreleases/2023/september/christopher-m-reddy-honored-with-acs-2024-grady-stack-award.html |publisher=American Chemical Society |access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref> 

===Science communication===

Reddy reportedly views communication of scientific matters to diverse audiences and "building connections between the scientific community and societal stakeholders" to be important parts of being a scientist and has sought to develop and communicate this skill to peers and students.<ref name="ACS2024" /> He received the 2023 James T. Grady-James H. Stack Award for Interpreting Chemistry for the Public<ref name="Stack Award" /> and the 2018 [[American Geophysical Union|GSU]] Ambassador Award<ref name="ambassador" /> 

Reddy's efforts extend to influencing the next generation of scientists, and he collaborates on a [[science communication]] graduate course taught at [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution|WHOI]] titled "How Not to Write for Peer-Reviewed Journals: Talking to Everyone Else."<ref name="Stack Award" /> 

Effective communication of scientific information to nonscientists is even more important during a crisis such as the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill|''Deepwater Horizon'' oil spill]], Reddy believes, and has been the subject of talks (e.g., his [[TEDx]] talk using clips from the original [[Star Trek: The Original Series|''Star Trek'']] television series<ref name="star trek" />) and his book, ''Science Communication in a Crisis: An Insider's Guide''.<ref name="book" />  The latter, which is intended "to help scientists understand how best to communicate their knowledge and expertise in the event of an environmental crisis,"<ref>{{cite news |last=Geist |first=Gilda |date=15 September 2023 |title=Woods Hole Chemist Honored For Science Communication |url=https://www.capenews.net/falmouth/news/woods-hole-chemist-honored-for-science-communication/article_8a3fbe54-66f1-5a34-8fb3-1962a9ec444b.html |work=The Enterprise |location=Falmouth, MA |publisher=Mark Olivieri |access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref> draws on Reddy's years of responding to environmental crises and communicating actionable information to peers, journalists, regulators, and the public. John E. Riutta, author of ''The Well-Read Naturalist'', describes the book as "a collection of analyses and recommendations for those ... faced with presenting important scientific information to audiences both large and small during times of profound uncertainty" and terms it "very timely" given "the many destructive environmental and medical crises" that have occurred over recent decades.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Riutta |first1=John E. |title=Natural History Book Review|url=https://www.wellreadnaturalist.com/2023/06/science-communication-in-a-crisis/ |website=wellreadnaturalist.com |date=22 June 2023 |publisher=The Well-Read Naturalist |access-date=14 January 2025}}</ref>

==Publications==
Reddy published around 500 pieces in academic journals.<ref name="gs">{{cite web |title=Christopher Reddy |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=stbDzOgAAAAJ |publisher=Google Scholar |website=Google Scholar |access-date=20 January 2025}}</ref>

Reddy wrote two books: ''Science Communication in a Crisis: An Insider's Guide''<ref name="book" /> and one of the ''A Kids Book About'' children's series titled ''A Kids Book About Being a Scientist''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Reddy |first1=Christopher M. |title=A Kids Book About Being a Scientist |date=21 May 2024 |publisher=A Kid's Book About |location=Portland, OR | isbn=979-8892810746 |url=https://akidsco.com/products/a-kids-book-about-being-a-scientist |access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref>
